title: Two Ways to Read a Draft

beats.speaker: host
beats.say: When two people review the same draft, what should the first speaker ask before either voice starts explaining?

beats.speaker: guest
beats.say: Ask where the listener is most likely to lose the thread. That question forces the explanation to begin with the difficult connection, while the rest of the material can wait until the listener has a reason to care about each detail.

beats.speaker: host
beats.say: How does the second voice help?

beats.speaker: guest
beats.say: A distinct voice gives the listener a clean signal that the conversation has changed direction. The handoff also creates room for a new example or qualification without making one speaker carry every transition inside a single unbroken explanation.

beats.speaker: guest
beats.say: They can challenge an assumption when the source supports that challenge, because useful tension helps the listener see where a decision carries risk, but neither host should invent a position merely to make the exchange sound lively.

beats.speaker: host
beats.say: What keeps the exchange from sounding staged?

beats.speaker: guest
beats.say: Every turn needs to add a fact, sharpen a question, qualify a claim, or connect two ideas that were difficult to hold together, so greetings and automatic agreement disappear before the voices ever reach the microphone.
